o: Each cheese must go to exactly one mouse; mouse 1 eats exactly `k` cheeses. We want the maximum total points. The baseline idea: give every cheese to mouse 2 (`sum(reward2)`), then decide which `k` cheeses to switch to mouse 1. Switching cheese `i` changes the total by `reward1[i] - reward2[i]`, so we should switch the `k` cheeses with the largest positive differences. In example 1, differences are [-3,-3,2,3]; picking indices 2 and 3 gives sum(reward2)=10 + 2 + 3 = 15. With n up to 1e5 we need an O(n log n) approach.
k: Reframe as: start with all cheese on mouse 2, then gain reward1[i]-reward2[i] for each switched cheese.
Pick the k largest differences greedily.

a.i: The total is sum(reward2) plus the gains from the k cheeses moved to mouse 1. Since choices are independent, sorting the differences and taking the top k is optimal.
s: Sort diff descending and add the first k values.

a.i: Instead of full sorting, keep a min-heap of the k largest differences seen so far; final heap contents are the top-k gains.
s: Push each difference into a min-heap; pop when size exceeds k.
Sum remaining heap entries plus sum(reward2).

w: Use the sorting version in an interview — it's simplest and fast enough. Pitfall: forgetting that negative differences still may be forced when k is large (taking top-k handles this automatically). Edge cases: k=0 (answer is sum(reward2)) and k=n (answer is sum(reward1)). Follow-up: what if each mouse has its own required count — same technique generalizes.
